title: What an Employee Takes Away in Memory
paragraphs: Trade-secret law protects information that derives economic value from not being generally known, and it has never been controversial that an employer may prevent a departing employee from carrying off customer lists, chemical formulas, or source code. The difficulty arises when what leaves is not a document but a memory. A substantial line of decisions treats memorized information as protectable on the same footing as copied files, reasoning that the injury to the employer is identical however the information travels, and that a rule turning on the method of taking would reward only those with good recall. The reasoning is tidy, and for a certain class of information it is also correct.

Yet the equation of memory with documents rests on a premise that deserves scrutiny: that everything an employee remembers is information in the same sense. Some of it is. A chemist who can recite from memory the fourteen proportions of a proprietary dye has taken a discrete, identifiable item that the employer could have written down and kept locked in a drawer. But much of what a long-serving employee carries is of another kind: a trained sense of when a dye bath is ready, an intuition about which suppliers deliver late, a feel for what clients will tolerate. Such knowledge cannot be recited, could not have been locked away, and is largely indistinguishable from the skill the employee brings to any later employer. To restrain it is to restrain the person.

Henrietta Vass, the most influential defender of the broad rule, answers that the distinction is unadministrable. Any former employee sued over a rival venture, she observes, will claim to be using only general skill, and courts cannot look inside a skull to test the claim. The objection has force, but it proves less than Vass supposes. Courts routinely infer intentions from conduct, and the conduct here is often revealing: an employee who spends her final weeks reciting formulas into a notebook has left a trail that no claim of mere general skill can explain. Requiring the employer to identify the particular information alleged to have been taken, moreover, ties the inquiry to something a court can actually examine.

The stakes of getting the line wrong are not symmetrical. An overbroad rule does not merely burden individual workers; it lowers the rate at which skills move among firms, and with them the ideas that tend to travel in skilled heads. Regions whose courts have enforced the broad rule vigorously have, on some accounts, seen their younger firms struggle to hire experienced staff, though the evidence is too thin to be conclusive. What the law should ask, then, is not through what medium information left the employer's control but what kind of thing left. Protection should attach to discrete items that the employer has taken reasonable steps to keep secret, whether the employee copied them or merely memorized them, and should stop where secrecy gives way to the general competence that is the employee's own.

viewpoints.position: Memorized information is protectable on the same footing as copied documents, since the employer's injury is the same.
A distinction between secrets and general skill cannot be administered, because courts cannot test an employee's claim to be using only skill.
Law should restrain use of discrete, identifiable secrets even when memorized, but not the general competence that belongs to the employee.

lowResSummary: Author argues trade-secret law should bar use of memorized discrete secrets but not general skill, answering a critic who says that line cannot be administered.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.A: Courts should treat memorized information as protectable on the same footing as copied documents, because the injury to an employer is identical however the information leaves.
choices.B: Trade-secret law should not reach anything that an employee carries in memory, since restraining memory amounts to restraining the person herself and discouraging the movement of skilled workers between firms.
choices.C: Because courts cannot inspect an employee's mind, trade-secret law should restrain departing employees only when they have actually copied documents rather than relied on memory.
choices.D: Trade-secret law should restrain a departing employee from using discrete, identifiable secrets even when memorized, but not the general skill and judgment that are her own.
choices.E: Restraints on departing employees slow the movement of skilled workers among firms, and for that reason the scope of trade-secret protection should be narrowed.

explanations.A: Opposite. This is the position of the line of decisions that the author qualifies; it is correct only 'for a certain class of information.'
explanations.B: Extreme. The author grants that the chemist who recites fourteen proportions has 'taken a discrete, identifiable item,' which the law may protect even though it was memorized.
explanations.C: Reversal. This is the view the author rejects: protection should attach 'whether the employee copied them or merely memorized them.'
explanations.D: Correct. The final paragraph says protection should attach to discrete, secret items 'whether the employee copied them or merely memorized them,' and 'stop where secrecy gives way to the general competence that is the employee's own.'
explanations.E: Wrong part. The mobility point is a consideration in the fourth paragraph, hedged as resting on 'thin' evidence, not the thesis.

questions.keyTakeaway: The thesis has two halves, what is restrained and what is left free; wrong answers usually keep only one half or swap them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a chemist who recites from memory the fourteen proportions of a proprietary dye has

choices.A: taken a discrete, identifiable item that the employer could have written down and kept locked away
choices.B: shown the kind of skill that cannot be separated from her general competence as a chemist or from what she would bring to any later employer
choices.C: violated trade-secret law, whether or not the employer had taken steps to keep the proportions secret
choices.D: acquired knowledge that courts have generally declined to treat as protectable by the employer
choices.E: gained a trained sense of when a dye bath is ready for use in later employment

explanations.A: Correct. Paragraph 2: 'a discrete, identifiable item that the employer could have written down and kept locked in a drawer.'
explanations.B: Wrong part. This describes the second kind of knowledge, the 'trained sense,' not the recited proportions.
explanations.C: Extreme. The author's final paragraph requires that the employer 'has taken reasonable steps to keep secret' the items; the passage does not say any recitation is a violation.
explanations.D: Opposite. Paragraph 1 says a substantial line of decisions does treat memorized information as protectable.
explanations.E: Shell game. A trained sense of when a dye bath is ready is offered as an example of the other kind of knowledge, not as what the chemist has taken.

questions.keyTakeaway: The dye example is built to contrast two kinds of knowledge; keep track of which example belongs to which kind.

questions.stem: The author mentions an employee who spends her final weeks reciting formulas into a notebook primarily in order to

choices.A: illustrate the kind of general skill that employers cannot legitimately restrain a former employee from using
choices.B: concede that courts have no means of determining what a departing employee has retained in memory
choices.C: show that an employee's reliance on protected information can sometimes be inferred from observable conduct
choices.D: support the claim that memorized information should be treated in the same way as copied documents
choices.E: argue that employers ought to monitor the activities of employees who have given notice of departure

explanations.A: Opposite. The notebook conduct is described as something 'no claim of mere general skill can explain.'
explanations.B: Half right. The author concedes that the objection 'has force,' but the example is offered to show that courts can sometimes tell, not that they cannot.
explanations.C: Correct. The example answers Vass: 'Courts routinely infer intentions from conduct, and the conduct here is often revealing.'
explanations.D: Wrong force. The example is used to defend a distinction between secrets and skill, not to equate memory with documents.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The passage recommends no monitoring by employers.

questions.keyTakeaway: An illustration inside a rebuttal serves the rebuttal; ask which claim of the opponent the example is meant to answer.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Vass would be most likely to agree that

choices.A: an employee who recites formulas into a notebook before resigning should be presumed to be using only general skill
choices.B: restraints on departing employees should be confined to information that the employee has copied rather than memorized
choices.C: the skill that an employee develops during a long tenure properly belongs to the employer that paid for the training
choices.D: an employer seeking to restrain a former employee should be required to identify the particular information alleged to have been taken before the court considers any restraint
choices.E: a court asked whether a former employee is using only general skill would have no direct means of testing the employee's claim

explanations.A: Opposite. Vass defends the broad rule; she would not presume innocence from such conduct.
explanations.B: Reversal. Vass defends treating memory like documents, so she would not confine restraints to copied material.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Vass's objection concerns administrability, and nothing is said about who owns trained skill.
explanations.D: Wrong part. The identification requirement is the author's own proposal in reply to Vass.
explanations.E: Correct. Vass observes that a former employee 'will claim to be using only general skill, and courts cannot look inside a skull to test the claim.'

questions.keyTakeaway: To predict a critic's view, restate her stated objection and ask which choice is a direct consequence of it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following would the author be most likely to regard as information that trade-secret law may legitimately restrain a departing employee from using?

choices.A: a salesperson's sense, built up over years, of which buyers will accept a price increase
choices.B: a table of negotiated discount rates for three hundred clients that the employer kept confidential and that the employee deliberately memorized before leaving
choices.C: an engineer's ability to diagnose faults in a class of machinery after a decade of maintaining it
choices.D: a manager's general understanding of which suppliers in the region tend to deliver late
choices.E: a price list that the employer published to all its customers and that the employee remembers accurately

explanations.A: Wrong part. A built-up sense of what clients will tolerate is the kind of knowledge the author says cannot be restrained.
explanations.B: Correct. It is a discrete, identifiable item that the employer took reasonable steps to keep secret, and the author says protection applies 'whether the employee copied them or merely memorized them.'
explanations.C: Wrong part. Diagnostic ability is general skill, 'largely indistinguishable' from what the employee brings to any later employer.
explanations.D: Wrong part. An 'intuition about which suppliers deliver late' is one of the author's own examples of unrestrainable knowledge.
explanations.E: Shell game. A published list is not secret, so it fails the author's condition that the employer took 'reasonable steps to keep secret' the item.

questions.keyTakeaway: Apply the author's two-part test: a discrete item, and one the employer actually kept secret.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Vass's objection can most accurately be described as

choices.A: acknowledgment that it has some force, combined with the view that it establishes less than Vass claims
choices.B: complete agreement, since it shows that the proposed distinction cannot be administered by courts
choices.C: scornful dismissal, since it ignores the difficulty of proving what an employee has memorized and the cost of litigating such claims
choices.D: indifference, since it concerns a question that the author regards as irrelevant to the thesis
choices.E: reluctant acceptance, since the author concedes that the distinction must be abandoned in practice

explanations.A: Correct. 'The objection has force, but it proves less than Vass supposes.'
explanations.B: Opposite. The author goes on to argue that the distinction can be administered.
explanations.C: Extreme. The author grants that the objection 'has force' and does not dismiss it with scorn.
explanations.D: Out of scope. The objection is answered at length and bears directly on the thesis.
explanations.E: Extreme. The author keeps the distinction and explains how courts can apply it.

questions.keyTakeaway: 'Has force, but' is the signature of qualified disagreement.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's suggestion that vigorous enforcement of the broad rule impedes younger firms?

choices.A: Younger firms in regions of vigorous enforcement spend more on training new employees than older firms in the same regions do.
choices.B: The proportion of new firms that survive their first five years is the same in regions of vigorous enforcement as elsewhere.
choices.C: When one region's courts narrowed the broad rule, its younger firms hired markedly more experienced staff, while comparable regions that kept the rule saw no such rise.
choices.D: Experienced employees in regions of vigorous enforcement are more likely than employees elsewhere to be sued by their former employers.
choices.E: Younger firms in regions of vigorous enforcement have always been concentrated in industries that employ few experienced workers of any kind.

explanations.A: True but irrelevant. Higher training spending is consistent with the claim but does not show that enforcement caused the hiring difficulty.
explanations.B: Wrong force. Equal survival rates, if anything, count against a harm to younger firms; at best they are neutral on hiring.
explanations.C: Correct. A change in enforcement followed by a change in hiring, with comparable regions as controls, supports a causal link between the rule and the difficulty.
explanations.D: True but irrelevant. Frequency of lawsuits does not show that younger firms struggle to hire.
explanations.E: Opposite. It supplies an alternative explanation for the hiring difficulty that does not depend on enforcement.

questions.keyTakeaway: The best support for a causal claim varies the cause and shows the effect following, with a comparison group that did not change.
